extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society / experimental natural philosophers, astronomers, and botanists (late-17th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Reports and commentary on experimental and observational natural philosophy (astronomy, botany, mechanics), describing methods, measurements, and reasoning used to verify hypotheses and explain phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental verification with great exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments are tried with pendula 'in order to verify the foregoing speculation, and to determine the quantity of the air's opposition to bodies moving in it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments should be performed with great exactness to test theoretical speculation and to quantify forces (e.g., air resistance). Includes performing several experiments and reporting measured quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical demonstrations must explain principal phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrations of preceding books are applied 'to the explication of the principal phaenomena of nature' and give 'a full resolution given to all the difficulties that occur in the astronomical science.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory theory should derive observed phenomena (e.g., tides, spheroidal figure of earth, precession) from its hypotheses and resolve outstanding difficulties; it should make the necessary consequences explicit and computable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of approximations with error-awareness (cometary orbits)
rubrics_metrics.description: A general method is laid down to determine trajectories of comets 'upon supposition that those curves are parabolic, or so near it that the parabola may serve without sensible error; though it be more probable... that these orbits are elliptical.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods may use simplifying assumptions (parabolic approximation) but should note probable true form (elliptical) and justify that approximation's adequacy and limitations relative to observational error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical observations must determine mean distances, motions, and epochs
rubrics_metrics.description: Cassini determined mean distances of Saturn's satellites, their diurnal motions, durations of conjunctions, and epochs (e.g., 'he determined its mean distance... and its diurnal motion at ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational reports should provide measured mean distances, angular motions, conjunction durations, and reference epochs so that tables and ephemerides can be constructed; note practical difficulties (distinguishing similar satellites).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments with controls, repeated observations, and long-term follow-up (tree growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations on trees include ring-barking, pruning, and comparison with unpruned trees over several years, noting both growth increase and eventual death ('the 3d year it died', 'in 7 or 8 years time, the difference is prodigious').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental interventions (e.g., bark-cutting, pruning) should record treatment details (dimensions, timing), include comparison with untreated controls, be observed across multiple seasons/years, and report survival, growth increments, and timing (season of operation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report environmental/contextual conditions and timing of interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual time for making this section was 'either in March or the beginning of April'; observations also relate to effects of a severe frost in 1684 on pruned vs unpruned trees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record season, weather events, and other environmental factors that could affect outcomes; relate treatments to vulnerability under specific climatic events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw mechanism hypotheses from aggregated observations
rubrics_metrics.description: From experiments the author infers that 'the sap (most of it, if not all) ascends in the vessels of the ligneous part... that the increase and growth of a tree in thickness is by the descent of the sap... that there is a continual circulation of the sap all the summer season.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated, corroborating observations to propose mechanistic accounts (e.g., pathways and circulation of sap), and state those mechanisms as hypotheses tied to empirical findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations of perceptual phenomena must reconcile geometry, physiology, and imagination and be testable
rubrics_metrics.description: On the moon's apparent enlargement near the horizon: critiques of Descartes, Gassendus, Hobbes, and the Abbe emphasize geometric scale, pupil/crystalline physiology, refraction, and the imagination's use of intermediate objects as potential explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory account of a perceptual illusion should: (a) be consistent with geometric optics; (b) properly model physiological optics (pupil size, crystalline lens, retinal projection); (c) account for psychological/imaginative estimations using intermediate visual cues; and (d) be testable by instrumented measurement (e.g., sextant, telescope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use instruments and accurate experimental prosecution to adjudicate perceptual disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Caswell, Vallis, and others assert that instrument measures (sextant, telescope) show horizontal diameters are not greater; author criticizes Riccioli's experiments as insufficiently prosecuted and urges testing when the horizontal moon 'had looked 10 times larger'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve disagreements between naked-eye impressions and theory by careful instrumented measurement; design experiments to include extreme perceived cases and ensure accurate, reproducible procedures to avoid mistaken inferences from casual observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure geometric models respect real-world scale and reference points
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Hobbes' geometric construction: 'he has made the circle GF, representing the earth, very large in proportion to the circle AD' and thus misapplies the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using geometric constructions to explain perception or physical relations, choose scales and reference points that reflect the actual geometry (e.g., treat the earth as negligible compared to the sphere of fixed stars where appropriate), otherwise conclusions may be invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish direct projection from refractive imaging when reasoning about aperture effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterargument to Faber/Gassendus: while a larger aperture gives a larger projection in direct (pinhole) projections, in refractive imaging (the eye, telescope) narrowing the pupil does not change image size though it affects brightness and definition ('no more is affected by this narrow aperture, but only that the sides of the radiating cones are intercepted...it shall still be in the same place').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optical reasoning must account for refraction by lenses (crystalline, objective) versus simple hole-projection; conclusions about image size, brightness, and resolving power depend on the imaging regime and must be justified accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational methods should minimize bias and be designed for the phenomenon's extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Author notes Riccioli should have tried his sextant experiments 'when the horizontal moon had looked 10 times larger in diameter than ordinary' to test claims that instruments measure larger diameters at the horizon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design observational tests to include extreme instances of the claimed effect, ensure measurement methods are sensitive enough to detect the magnitude of claimed differences, and beware of systematic biases introduced by the measurement procedure or observers' methods (e.g., edge-marking by two observers).
